answer: On the raw features, η = 0.1 made the loss explode to inf within 12 steps (η = 0.001 converged but needed ~40,000 iterations; η = 0.01 was the best raw-feature compromise). Your lesson: look at feature scales before blaming the learning rate.

question: Q03
answer: Three notes together: (1) note-gaussian-noise-least-squares shows that with Gaussian noise the maximum-likelihood fit is exactly least squares; (2) note-map-estimation-priors shows that MAP = likelihood + log-prior, and with an isotropic Gaussian prior θ ~ N(0, τ²I) the log-prior is −‖θ‖²/(2τ²), so with the Gaussian-noise likelihood the objective becomes squared error + (σ²/τ²)‖θ‖²; (3) note-ridge-regression-penalty is exactly that objective, ‖y − Xw‖² + λ‖w‖². Link in one paragraph: minimizing squared error is maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise; adding a Gaussian prior on the weights and maximizing the posterior instead adds −log p(w) = ‖w‖²/(2τ²) to the negative log-likelihood, so the MAP estimate is the ridge estimate with λ = σ²/τ² — a narrow prior (small τ) means a large penalty, a flat prior (τ → ∞) gives back plain least squares. This also answers the open question you left in the ridge note ('Where does λ come from … does it mean something?'), although neither note links to the other. note-lasso-sparsity-geometry plus the last line of the MAP note (Laplace prior → Σ|θ_j|) give the L1 counterpart.

evidence.quote: If the likelihood is the Gaussian-noise linear model, the first term is the sum of squared residuals over 2σ², so the whole thing is squared error plus a constant times ‖θ‖², with the constant being σ²/τ² after rescaling.
Where does λ come from — is it just a knob you tune by cross-validation, or does it mean something?
